content.objectives: Classify natural, integer, rational, irrational and real numbers; explain the nesting of number systems.
content.reading: Number systems grow when an old set cannot support a needed operation. Natural numbers count. Integers make subtraction below zero possible. Rational numbers support division into fractions. Real numbers include irrational measurements such as √2.
content.deep_explanation:
N ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R.
A terminating or recurring decimal is rational. An irrational decimal neither terminates nor repeats. Always classify a value in the smallest standard set that contains it.
content.examples:
0.272727…=27/99=3/11, so it is rational.

Since 49<50<64, 7<√50<8; √50 is irrational.
content.practice: Classify each in the smallest set: 7, −4, 2/3, 0.125, √7. Explain why recurring decimals are rational.
content.practice_answers: 7 natural; −4 integer; 2/3 rational; 0.125 rational; √7 irrational. A recurring decimal can be converted to a ratio of integers by place-value subtraction.
content.summary: Larger sets solve limitations of smaller ones. Decimal appearance alone does not decide rationality.
